newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl hints he may consider his future this year.
newsitem.headline: Kohl hints he may consider his future this year.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl, one of the fiercest champions of closer European unity, has given his strongest hint yet that he is seriously thinking of retiring, perhaps even this year.

The 66-year-old chancellor, used to keeping Germans guessing about how long he will stay in office, has been widely believed to want at least to bring to fruition the historic project of EU monetary union, due to start in 1999, before calling it a day.
In an interview on French television on Sunday, however, Kohl said he had not yet decided whether to stand again in the October 1998 general election.
As a goal he wanted to achieve, he named the successful conclusion of the EU's Maastricht Treaty reform summit in Amsterdam in June.
"Then I will discuss it (whether to stand again) with my political friends," Kohl said.

"I want to do my duty, and I will have to decide for myself, in conversation with my closest relatives, with my family and my political friends. And that conversation does not have to take place yet," he said.

As Europe's longest-serving head of government, Kohl's political role in European integration has been almost as pivotal as that played by the German mark, the anchor for the European exchange rate system.
To markets, he provided the best guarantee that sceptical Germans can be persuaded that Kohl's single currency project is worth giving up their cherished deutschemark for.

Domestically, he was seen within his party until the start of this year as the one man to guarantee the Christian Democrats (CDU) would return to power at the head of their centre-right coalition with the liberal Free Democrats in October 1998.

But runaway unemployment and economic gloom, combined with the need to keep budget spending on a tight rein to allow Germany to qualify for EMU, have failed to produce either fighting form or new ideas from Kohl.

Meanwhile Wolfgang Schaeuble, the CDU parliamentary leader widely seen as Kohl's preferred successor, said in an interview that the chancellor's job was probably not one he would be able to resist if the chance arose. The comment is unlikely to have been made without Kohl's blessing.

For critical party officials, the issue is less whether Kohl is needed to see EMU into being, and more whether he has what it takes to convince voters he can get unemployment down and safeguard their pensions.

Two projects to reform the tax and pensions systems, far from giving the party flagship policies to see it through the election, have unleashed a storm of internal criticism, some of it aimed perilously close to the chancellor himself.

Those goals are also proving harder and harder to reconcile with the budget austerity needed to set the right example to the rest of the EU and make the "euro" credible to Germans as a currency that will be as stable as the mark.
"This time the feeling is spreading even within the CDU that Kohl no longer has the strength to overcome the latest crisis," wrote the left-liberal weekly Der Spiegel.

It is not yet clear who Kohl's main opponent would be in the 1998 election -- but there is a fair chance it could be Gerhard Schroeder, the charismatic Lower Saxony premier who is one of the few mainstream German politicians to call EMU into question.
One poll in January indicated that if Germans were able to choose their chancellor in a direct election, Schroeder would beat Kohl by 10 percentage points.

Der Spiegel said it was above all the prospect of a challenge from Schroeder that was making Schaeuble, ever Kohl's loyal lieutenant and perhaps Bonn's most astute politician, increasingly worried that Kohl might, at long last, no longer have what it takes.
